content: Zinc sulfide, chemically represented as ZnS, is a compound that appears as a white to yellow powder or crystal. It is most commonly found in its cubic crystalline form, which is also known as the mineral sphalerite. Another less common form of zinc sulfide is the hexagonal crystalline structure, referred to as the mineral wurtzite. Both sphalerite and wurtzite are intrinsic semiconductors with wide bandgaps. The cubic form (sphalerite) has a bandgap of 3.54 eV at a temperature of 300 K, while the hexagonal form (wurtzite) has a slightly larger bandgap of 3.91 eV. A phase transition from the cubic sphalerite structure to the hexagonal wurtzite structure occurs at approximately 1293.15 K. The melting point of sphalerite is 1991 K, and its standard enthalpy of formation is −204.6 kJ/mol at 298 K. Zinc sulfide has been historically significant in the field of nuclear physics. It was utilized by Ernest Rutherford and other early researchers as a scintillation detector due to its ability to emit light when excited by x-rays or electron beams. This property made it valuable for use in x-ray screens and cathode ray tubes. Additionally, zinc sulfide exhibits phosphorescence when exposed to blue or ultraviolet light, a property that arises from the presence of impurities. When doped with small amounts of specific activators, zinc sulfide becomes a phosphor material with various applications. For example, doping with silver produces a bright blue emission with a peak wavelength of 450 nm, while manganese doping results in an orange-red emission at approximately 590 nm. Copper doping is particularly notable for producing a greenish glow-in-the-dark effect with a long afterglow. Copper-doped zinc sulfide (ZnS+Cu) is also employed in electroluminescent panels. Zinc sulfide is further utilized as an infrared optical material, capable of transmitting light from visible wavelengths to beyond 12 micrometers. It can be manufactured into optical windows or lenses. The material is typically produced as microcrystalline sheets through a reaction involving hydrogen sulfide (H2S) gas and zinc vapor. This form, known as FLIR-grade ZnS, appears as a pale, milky yellow and is visibly opaque. When subjected to hot isostatic pressing (HIP), it can be transformed into a transparent, water-clear material marketed under the trademark Cleartran. Earlier commercial versions of this material were referred to as Irtran-2, though this term is now obsolete. Zinc sulfide is unique among II-VI semiconductors in that it can be doped to function as either an n-type or p-type semiconductor. Structurally, it is a covalently bonded solid. In laboratory settings, zinc sulfide can be synthesized by mixing zinc and sulfur in appropriate proportions and igniting the mixture. As the reaction subsides, zinc sulfide is formed. However, this process is highly exothermic and can be hazardous if not conducted with proper precautions.
